practiceItems.description: Two threads each transfer money between the same two accounts, but in opposite directions, and the program sometimes hangs forever. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that preserves correctness.
practiceItems.solution: This is deadlock: each thread holds one account's lock and waits for the other's. Fix it by imposing a single global lock order — for example, always lock the account with the smaller id first — so no thread can hold one lock while waiting for a lock another thread holds in the opposite order. Alternatives include using one lock per transfer operation, or tryLock with a timeout and retry, but a consistent lock order is the cleanest fix. Also verify with thread dumps that the hang is a lock cycle, not an infinite loop.
practiceItems.title: Deadlock in account transfers

practiceItems.description: A latency-sensitive service suffers periodic 2-second pauses, and GC logs show long old-generation collections. How do you investigate and reduce the pauses without guessing at flags?
practiceItems.solution: First confirm GC is the cause: enable GC logging (for example -Xlog:gc*) and correlate pause timestamps with the latency spikes. Then check what is being promoted: look for large short-lived allocations, oversized caches, or objects surviving because of long-lived references. Reduce allocation (reuse buffers, avoid boxing in hot paths, cap caches) before tuning the collector. If pauses remain, try a low-pause collector such as G1 with a pause-time goal or ZGC, and measure throughput and pause percentiles before and after — a collector change that fixes p99 at the cost of unacceptable throughput is not a win.
practiceItems.title: Diagnosing long GC pauses

practiceItems.description: A single-page app stores a long-lived JWT in localStorage and calls APIs with it. After a token theft incident, the team must redesign token handling. What should change, and what should stay?
practiceItems.solution: Move to short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus rotating refresh tokens: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is detected on reuse and the whole token family can be revoked. Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage where JavaScript can read it, and keep the short-lived access token in memory. Never put passwords, roles that must be revocable, or other sensitive data in the JWT payload, since it is only base64-encoded. Add a server-side revocation list or token version for immediate logout of compromised accounts.
practiceItems.title: Redesigning JWT handling after theft

practiceItems.description: A controller returns a JPA entity directly. The JSON serializer touches a lazily loaded collection and the request fails with LazyInitializationException in production but not in tests. Explain the difference and propose a fix.
practiceItems.solution: In tests the transaction (or Open Session in View) is often still open when serialization happens, so lazy loading succeeds; in production the transaction has closed before the serializer runs. Fix it properly: fetch exactly what the response needs inside the transaction — a JOIN FETCH query, an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — and return a DTO, not the entity. That also prevents leaking internal fields and accidental extra queries. Do not fix it by marking the association EAGER or by enabling Open Session in View in production, both of which hide the problem and cause unpredictable queries.
practiceItems.title: LazyInitializationException in production only

practiceItems.description: Checkout calls inventory, payment and notification services in sequence. When payment is slow, checkout threads block, timeouts cascade, and one slow service takes down the whole checkout flow. Propose a resilient design using timeouts, bulkheads and observability.
practiceItems.solution: Give every downstream call an explicit timeout (shorter than the caller's own timeout) so a slow service fails fast instead of holding threads. Isolate each dependency with a bulkhead — a dedicated thread pool or concurrency limit — so payment slowness cannot exhaust the pool used for inventory. Add a circuit breaker so repeated failures fail fast and recover gradually, and retry only idempotent calls with backoff and a cap. Make payment calls idempotent with an idempotency key so a retried request cannot double-charge. Expose health, metrics and traces (via Actuator and distributed tracing) so the slow dependency is visible before it cascades, and design the checkout to degrade gracefully — for example, queue the notification instead of blocking checkout on it.
practiceItems.title: Resilient checkout across microservices

practiceItems.description: A candidate answers 'Tell me about a time you handled a tight deadline' like this: 'We had a really busy period at work and everyone was stressed. The project was complicated and there were lots of stakeholders. We worked really hard and in the end we managed to deliver it, which was great.' A strong rewrite: Situation — a fictional reporting tool had to launch in two weeks when its data source changed format. Task — the candidate owned the data-import part. Action — mapped the format differences, proposed a translation layer instead of rewriting every report, built it behind a flag, and compared old and new outputs on sample data. Result — launched on the original date with matching outputs, and the translation layer made the next format change take hours instead of days. Lesson: check external source stability early in planning.

practiceItems.solution: Change the tone: describe the disagreement as a difference in view or priority, not as the teammate being wrong, and avoid blame or gossip. Change the structure: show listening first (what the teammate's concern was and why it was reasonable), then the discussion, then how a decision was reached. Change the ending: close with the resolution and the working relationship afterwards, plus what the candidate changed about how they handle disagreements — not with a victory lap.

practiceItems.description: An interviewer asks: 'What happens when your notification service goes down?' A candidate replies: 'It never goes down; we built it well.' Rewrite this into a strong deep-dive answer using a fictional booking system where notifications are sent asynchronously from a queue.
practiceItems.solution: A strong answer: bookings still succeed because the notification worker reads from a queue and is separate from the booking path, so a worker outage delays messages rather than losing bookings. On recovery, queued notifications are retried and delivered. Detection comes from queue-depth and worker-health alerts. The deliberate trade-off: delaying an email was judged acceptable, losing a booking was not. If the queue itself failed, bookings would still be recorded but notifications would need a replay from booking records — that is the residual risk, and it is why queue durability was chosen over speed.

practiceItems.description: Write a SQL query that returns each customer who has placed at least 3 non-cancelled orders, with their order count and total spend, ordered by total spend descending. Tables: customers (id, email), orders (id, customer_id, total_amount, status).

examples.input: orders: customer 1 has 4 orders totalling 500, customer 2 has 2 orders totalling 900
examples.output: Only customer 1 appears, with order_count 4 and total_spent 500

hints: Filter cancelled orders with WHERE before grouping.
Use GROUP BY customer_id with COUNT(*) and SUM(total_amount).
Filter groups with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3, not WHERE.
practiceItems.solution:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
practiceItems.prompt: Write a SQL query that returns each customer who has placed at least 3 non-cancelled orders, with their order count and total spend, ordered by total spend descending.

practiceItems.description: Write a SQL query that returns the id and email of every customer who has never placed an order. Tables: customers (id, email), orders (id, customer_id).

examples.input: customers 1 and 2; only customer 1 has an order

hints: Use a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders.
Filter for rows where the joined order side is NULL.
practiceItems.solution:
SELECT c.id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

practiceItems.description: Users report that after updating their profile name, the old name keeps showing for up to an hour. The profile is cached in Redis with a 1-hour TTL, and the update path writes to the database but does not touch the cache. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that keeps caching benefits.
practiceItems.solution: Diagnosis: the cache is stale because the update path never invalidates the cached entry, so reads keep serving the old value until the TTL expires. Fix: evict (or update) the cached profile key in the same code path that writes the database, for example with Spring's @CacheEvict on the update method keyed by user id. Keep the TTL as a safety net for any missed invalidation, and consider a shorter TTL for frequently changed profile data. Verify with a test that updates the profile and then reads it back through the cache.

practiceItems.description: You are modelling a blogging platform in MongoDB. Each post has comments, and popular posts can accumulate tens of thousands of comments over years. Should comments be embedded in the post document or stored as separate documents referenced by post id? Justify your choice and note the trade-off.
practiceItems.solution: Store comments as separate documents referenced by post id. Embedding suits bounded data read together with the parent, but a comment list that grows without bound will hit the 16 MB document limit, make every comment addition rewrite a huge document, and slow post reads that do not need comments. Referencing keeps post documents small and stable, lets comments be paginated and indexed independently, and costs an extra query (or aggregation) to load a page of comments, which is the correct trade-off here. A small embedded summary, such as a comment count, can be maintained on the post if needed.
practiceItems.prompt: You are modelling a blogging platform in MongoDB.

practiceItems.description: A team wants to move its order and payment data from PostgreSQL to a document store 'for scalability', although current load is modest and the main complaints are slow reports and occasional double-charges. Evaluate the proposal and recommend an approach.
practiceItems.solution: Do not migrate the transactional core: orders and payments need multi-row ACID transactions, integrity constraints, and join-heavy reporting, which PostgreSQL serves well and a document store serves poorly. The symptoms point elsewhere: slow reports suggest missing indexes or N+1-style query problems, and double-charges suggest missing idempotency or transaction boundaries, not the wrong database family. Fix those first, measure, and only consider a second store for a workload that genuinely fits it, such as a document store for the product catalogue or Redis for caching, keeping PostgreSQL as the system of record for orders and payments.

practiceItems.description: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application built with Maven. The build stage must compile the jar, the runtime stage must contain only a JRE and the jar, dependencies must be cached before source is copied, and the container must run as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint exposing port 8080.
examples: Input: a Maven project with pom.xml and src/ → Output: an image that runs the Spring Boot jar on port 8080 without Maven or source code in the final image
hints: Copy pom.xml and download dependencies in their own layer before copying src/.
Use COPY --from=build to bring only the jar into the runtime stage.
Create a user and switch to it with USER before ENTRYPOINT.
practiceItems.solution:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/myapp-1.0.0.jar app.jar
RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
practiceItems.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot

practiceItems.description: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on pushes to main and on pull requests, sets up JDK 21 with a Maven cache, runs the full build and tests, then builds and pushes a container image tagged with the commit SHA. Secrets must not appear in the file.

hints: Trigger on push to main and on pull_request.
Use actions/setup-java with java-version 21 and cache maven.
Tag the image with github.sha so every image traces to one commit.
practiceItems.solution:
name: build-and-test
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up JDK 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: "21"
          distribution: temurin
          cache: maven
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./mvnw -q verify
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }}

practiceItems.description: Write a Kubernetes Deployment for a Spring Boot service named order-service with 3 replicas, a pinned image version, container port 8080, a prod Spring profile via environment variable, memory and CPU requests and limits, and liveness and readiness probes using Actuator endpoints.
examples: Input: image <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0 → Output: 3 healthy replicas behind matching labels, receiving traffic only when ready
hints: The Deployment selector must match the pod template labels.
Use /actuator/health/liveness for liveness and /actuator/health/readiness for readiness.
Set requests for scheduling and limits as a cap, with heap sized inside the memory limit.
practiceItems.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "prod"
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "1Gi"
              cpu: "500m"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/liveness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/readiness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10

practiceItems.description: A teammate copied a credentials file into a Docker image in one layer and deleted it in a later layer, believing the secret was gone. The image was pushed to the registry. What is the real situation, and what must the team do now?
practiceItems.solution: The secret is still in the image: layers are immutable, and the earlier layer containing the file remains in the image history and can be retrieved. Deleting in a later layer only hides it from the final filesystem view. The team must rotate the exposed credential immediately, rebuild the image without the secret ever being copied in, push the clean image, and remove the tainted image from the registry. Going forward, secrets arrive at run time via environment variables or a secret store, never via COPY or ENV in a Dockerfile.

practiceItems.description: Your team's CI pipeline fails intermittently on the same few tests, and developers have started rerunning the pipeline until it goes green. What is wrong with this habit, and what should the team do instead?
practiceItems.solution: Retrying until green destroys trust in CI: real failures get retried away alongside flaky ones, and the suite stops being evidence that a change is safe. The team should quarantine the flaky tests, reproduce the flakiness, and fix the root cause — usually timing assumptions, shared mutable state, test-order dependence, or reliance on an external service. Only deterministic tests return to the suite, and a pattern of retries on one test is treated as a bug to fix, not a normal workflow.

practiceItems.description: After a rolling update on AWS, error rates spike for a Spring Boot service, but the new containers pass their basic liveness checks. How should the team respond, and what made a fast rollback possible?
practiceItems.solution: Roll back first and investigate second: redeploy the previous known-good image, which the rolling update kept available, rather than hot-fixing production under pressure. Liveness only proves the process is alive, not that it serves correctly, which is why error-rate and latency alarms, readiness checks, and smoke tests matter. The rollback was possible because images are tagged by version and kept in the registry, the previous task definition or Deployment revision was retained, and configuration is separate from the image, so the old image runs correctly with current configuration.

practiceItems.description: A test suite passes when tests are run individually but sometimes fails when the whole suite runs. One failing test reads the current date, another writes to a shared static map that a later test reads, and a third waits for an async job with Thread.sleep(200). Diagnose each failure source and propose a concrete fix for each, plus the process for handling the flaky tests in the meantime.
practiceItems.solution: All three are classic flakiness sources. (1) The date-dependent test should inject a java.time.Clock and use Clock.fixed in tests, so 'now' is controlled and repeatable. (2) The shared static map is shared mutable state: reset it in @BeforeEach (or remove the static sharing) so no test depends on execution order or another test's leftovers. (3) The Thread.sleep guess should be replaced by awaiting a condition with a timeout (e.g. Awaitility), so the test waits exactly until the async work completes. Process: quarantine the flaky tests so their failures do not block the suite, reproduce each (run the suite repeatedly), fix the root cause, and only then un-quarantine. Do not just delete them, which would silently lose coverage.
practiceItems.title: Diagnosing a flaky test suite

practiceItems.description: A repository test suite passes against the default embedded database in @DataJpaTest, but the same queries fail in production on PostgreSQL. Explain the likely cause, how to reproduce the failure in tests, and what changes to make to the test setup.
practiceItems.solution: The likely cause is a dialect difference: H2 tolerates SQL, types, or functions that PostgreSQL rejects (or vice versa), so the embedded database hides a real failure. Reproduce it by running the repository tests against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers: add a static @Container PostgreSQLContainer with @ServiceConnection, annotate the test with @Testcontainers, and set @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) on the @DataJpaTest so the container database is actually used instead of being silently replaced by H2. Pin the image tag to a major version (e.g. postgres:16). Keep these container tests focused on database-specific behaviour; the rest of the suite stays at cheaper layers.
practiceItems.title: Tests pass on H2 but fail on PostgreSQL
